name: View
first: A type that describes part of an app's user interface, with a body that says which views it is made of.

dependsOn.why: The views of a SwiftUI app are usually structures, whose stored properties hold the values they show.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `Greeting` is a structure, and its stored property `name` holds the name that it shows.

dependsOn.why: A view is a type that conforms to SwiftUI's view protocol, which requires a body.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `Greeting` conforms to the protocol `View`, and has the `body` that `View` requires.

dependsOn.why: The type of a view's body is an opaque type, so the body can return any view while its declaration names only the view protocol.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The type of `body` is `some View`. Its real type is `Text`, which swiftc works out from the body.

what.is: A view is a type that describes part of an app's user interface. It conforms to the protocol `View`, which requires one property, `body`, whose value is the views that this view is made of. A view is a description: SwiftUI reads it, and draws what it describes.
what.afterExample: `Greeting` describes a text that says hello to `name`. Its `body` returns a `Text`, a view that SwiftUI provides and draws itself.
what.problem: A screen is built from many parts, such as a title, a list, and a button. A view lets each part be written once, as a type, and used inside other views. SwiftUI reads the views and draws the screen from them, so the code says what the screen shows, not the steps that draw it.
what.how: SwiftUI reads a view's `body` to learn what the view is made of, and reads the `body` of each view inside it, down to views that SwiftUI draws itself, such as `Text`. Reading `body` makes no window and draws nothing: it returns a value that describes the views.

when.text: Use a view for each part of a screen that has a name and a job, such as a greeting, so that other views can use it by name, as `Greeting(name: "Ana")`.
Don't put work that takes long, or that changes data, in `body`. SwiftUI reads `body` each time it needs the description again, which can be often.

parts.name: The conformance to `View`, line 3
parts.text: The colon and the name `View` after `Greeting` say that `Greeting` conforms to the protocol `View`. `View` requires one property, `body`. SwiftUI can show any type that conforms to `View`.

parts.name: The property `body`, lines 5 to 7
parts.text: A computed property runs its code each time it is read, and returns a value. Lines 5 to 7 declare `body`, the computed property that `View` requires. Its type is `some View`, and here it returns a `Text` that says hello to `name`.

steps.text: Line 10 makes a `Greeting` with the name `"Ana"`, and stores it in `greeting`. Nothing is drawn: `greeting` is a value that holds one string.
Line 11 reads `greeting.body`. The code of `body` runs, and line 6 returns a `Text` that says hello to `name`.
Line 11 prints the type of the value that `body` returned: {{Text}}.

end.text: A view is a value that describes part of a user interface. Its `body` returns the views it is made of, and SwiftUI draws from that description.
